1.pericope_label: Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel: Joab pleads against the order

schools.summary: Henry grants that numbering a people is in itself no bad thing, since a shepherd may know the number of his flock, and lays the fault wholly on the pride of David’s heart, insisting the sin was David’s and he alone must bear the blame, while Satan is active in it to weaken the strength and eclipse the glory of God’s Israel.

Ellicott argues from the missing article that the adversary is the wrath of God rather than the enemy of mankind, reads the order to Joab as military from the agents deputed to carry it, and treats Joab’s protest as an abridgement of Samuel with an explanatory clause added; Delitzsch agrees the captains assisted Joab, finds the two accounts agreeing in the main points and in many of their terms, and defends the shorter form of the protest against the doubled phrase in Samuel.

Wesley stages the opening legally, with Satan standing before the Lord’s tribunal to accuse David and Israel and beg leave to tempt him, and answers Joab’s question about trespass with a rule, that God commonly punishes a people for the sins of their rulers because they are for the most part guilty of the same sins in one kind or another.

debates.question: Who moved David to number Israel?

sides.position: an adversary who is the wrath of God, since the Hebrew word lacks the article it takes when the enemy of mankind is meant, and the parallel ascribes the inciting to the anger of the Lord
Satan, whom God for wise and holy ends permitted to do it, since God is not the author of sin and tempts no man
Satan as accuser, standing before the Lord’s tribunal to beg permission to tempt the king

debates.question: Which account preserves the older form of Joab’s protest?

sides.position: this one, the doubled phrase in Samuel being that writer’s peculiarity
Samuel, which this text abridges, the clause about becoming a cause of trespass being the chronicler’s explanatory addition

outliers: Wesley alone explains the accuser’s posture, that standing is the position of accusers before human tribunals, and that scripture speaks of the things of God after the manner of men.
Ellicott alone notices that Samuel’s phrase for running over all the tribes uses the very word Satan uses in Job for his wanderings over the earth.
themes: a census counted as sin
an adversary with no article
pride in the number of a flock
a commander who argues with his king

4.pericope_label: Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel: the totals returned, with Levi and Benjamin uncounted

schools.summary: Ellicott supplies the route from the older book, draws a late date from the nine months and twenty days the work took, offers three ways of meeting the discrepant totals, and finds the exemption of a sacerdotal tribe natural in a census taken for military or political purposes, the work having expressly never been completed.

Clarke sets the two sets of figures side by side without adjudicating and reports the rabbinic explanation that Joab deliberately spared two tribes with an answer ready for each objection; Wesley makes the omission providence rather than policy, since God would not have the tribes diminished that would stay faithful to the house of David, while allowing Joab his specious pretences too.

debates.question: Why do the totals differ from the parallel account?

sides.position: Judah’s figure there is a round number and this one more exact; behind the larger gap lies either an error of transcription or, more probably, varying traditions, since the numbers were never registered in the royal archives — though his own preference is that this total adds David’s standing army to the older figure
the figures are reported side by side, with no attempt to reconcile them

debates.question: Why were Levi and Benjamin left uncounted?

sides.position: a natural exemption, and an unfinished job: Joab, having numbered Judah, returned to the capital and was ordered to desist
calculated mercy: foreseeing the destruction the census would bring, Joab purposed to save two tribes
holders: the rabbis, reported by Adam Clarke

sides.position: providence, Levi being devoted to God’s service and Benjamin once almost extinguished, with Joab’s pretences serving as cover

outliers: Ellicott alone dates the census from the time it took, since only settled peace could have given the commander of the forces and his chief officers leisure for nine months and twenty days of it.
Ellicott alone cites Josephus, who speaks as though Joab had simply not had time for Benjamin and may have feared to give offence to the tribe of Saul.
themes: a route from Jordan round to Beersheba
numbers that will not reconcile
two tribes missing from the muster
a count stopped before it ends

7.pericope_label: God was displeased with this thing: the three judgments offered, and David in a great strait

schools.summary: Henry reads the whole passage as a man under the rod for the foolishness of pride, holds that no sin is more displeasing to God than pride of heart and nothing more mortifying to a gracious soul than to lie under that displeasure, sees the choice of three judgments as a further humiliation, and closes with the rule that good men think well of God even when he frowns upon them.

Ellicott treats the verse of displeasure as a general heading with no counterpart in Samuel, tracks the chronicler’s substitutions and explanatory additions through the confession and the prophet’s commission, illustrates the three penalties from the Annals of Tiglath Pileser I, prefers three years of famine to Samuel’s seven, and reads David’s answer as a confession of inability to choose.

Wesley names the motive the narrative leaves implicit, that the numbering was done without any colour of necessity, out of mere curiosity and ostentation; Clarke notes the divergence over the years of famine and preserves the Targum’s reconstruction of David’s reasoning, in which both famine and flight would expose him to his people’s reproach.

debates.question: How many years of famine were offered?

sides.position: three, which harmonises with the three months and the three days, Samuel’s seven having perhaps originated in a scribe’s memory of the Egyptian famine
the seven years of Samuel are registered without adjudication

debates.question: Why did David leave the choice to God?

sides.position: he confesses inability to choose, clear only that it is better to depend on the compassion of God than of man, which rules out the second alternative and leaves the rest to God

the Targum’s reasoning: famine would have his granaries thrown back at him and flight would have him called a warlike man careless of his people, so he delivers himself into the hand of the Word of the Lord
holders: the Targum, reported by Adam Clarke

sides.position: he cast himself on the mercy of God without entertaining hard thoughts of him

debates.question: Does this fuller text expand Samuel, or does Samuel epitomise it?

sides.position: ours looks like an exegetical expansion of the older and briefer statement
this is the original of which Samuel is an epitome, since otherwise the angel is introduced quite abruptly there

outliers: Ellicott alone infers from a later notice of Gad’s writings that it was Gad who composed the original record of the census.
Ellicott alone illustrates the three penalties from outside the Bible, with an Assyrian royal curse calling down the overthrow of an army, pestilence to cut off a land, and want of crops.
themes: a verdict printed before the story
three judgments and no good choice
a seer who may have written the record he reports
mercies many, and men’s hands few

14.pericope_label: There fell of Israel seventy thousand men: the destroying angel halted over Jerusalem

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the toll is abridged here and that Samuel supplies the plague’s duration, treats the stay of the angel as a textual problem in which Samuel’s reading is probably right, argues that Jerusalem itself was never touched, defends the vision against the charge of being a late embellishment, and suspects two marginal glosses in the closing words of David’s plea; Delitzsch holds that the Chronicle tells the sequence at greater length while corresponding in substance, preserving subordinate circumstances Samuel passes over.

Clarke turns aside to the Targum, where the angel beholds the ashes of the binding of Isaac and God remembers the covenant with Abraham and the image of Jacob on the throne of glory and countermands the destruction; Wesley reads the toll as the answer to the pride that provoked it and the sackcloth as men humbling themselves and deprecating the wrath against the people.

debates.question: Did the chronicler embellish the vision of the angel, or did Samuel abridge it?

sides.position: nothing in the style suggests a later hand, and it is as likely that the compiler of Samuel abridged the original account
the two accounts perfectly correspond in substance, the Chronicle merely keeping minor circumstances the other passes over

debates.question: What accounts for the sudden countermand?

sides.position: the merits of the fathers, set out at length in the Targum: the ashes of the binding of Isaac, the covenant made in the Mount of Worship, and the image of Jacob fixed on the throne of glory
holders: the Targum, reported by Adam Clarke

sides.position: a textual rather than a theological matter: the clause about the Lord beholding is absent from Samuel and, on Bertheau’s judgment, softens the harshness of the transition from command to countermand

outliers: Ellicott alone holds that it does not appear Jerusalem was touched at all.
Ellicott alone collects the variant spellings of the owner’s name across the versions and treats such differences as natural in foreign names.
themes: a plague that ran till the evening sacrifice
an angel between earth and heaven
elders in sackcloth on their faces
a shepherd asking what the sheep have done

18.pericope_label: Set up an altar unto the Lord in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite: the command, and the approach

schools.summary: Henry makes the double mediation the point, the angel who had carried on the war being the first to set the treaty of peace on foot and passing the word through the seer so as to put an honour upon the prophetic office; he reads the command to build as itself the pardon, keeps the angel as what Ornan saw, and notes that David would not serve God at other people’s charge.

Ellicott renders the angel’s word to Gad as a pluperfect, observes that Samuel knows nothing of the angel’s mediation and treats such mediation as a mark of the later books of the Canon, judges the Hebrew about what Ornan saw corrupt against the versions, thinks the clause about threshing wheat genuine nonetheless, and hears the purchase of Machpelah behind David’s stipulation of a full price.

Clarke assembles the versional and manuscript evidence for reading king instead of angel, with Houbigant’s reconstruction of two separate moments of sighting; Wesley keeps the angel, explaining that men’s weak natures cannot bear such glory and that the family feared the vengeance coming upon them, and joins Henry in reading the order to build as a token of reconciliation.

debates.question: Whom did Ornan see when he turned and looked?

sides.position: the king and his servants: the Hebrew here is corrupt, the words for angel and king being easily confused, and the versions and one of Kennicott’s manuscripts read king
the angel, whose brightness his weak nature could not bear, so that he and his four sons hid themselves

debates.question: Why did the order come through an angel and a prophet rather than directly?

sides.position: to put an honour upon the prophetic office, the angel being forward to open the treaty of peace he had been waging war against
the angel’s mediation is a feature of the later books, and Samuel has Gad simply coming to David that day

outliers: Henry alone draws the practical rule, that David would not serve God at other people’s charge.

Clarke alone reports Houbigant’s reconstruction, on which the two verses describe the king sighted at a distance and then arriving in the floor, so that the family hid and then had to present themselves.
themes: a destroying angel turned negotiator
one tittle of difference
a man threshing wheat in the path of a plague
a full price named before it is offered

23.pericope_label: I will verily buy it for the full price: the purchase, the altar, and the answer by fire

schools.summary: Ellicott reads Ornan’s enlarged offer and David’s firmer refusal as the chronicler filling out a shorter original, states the discrepancy between six hundred shekels of gold and fifty of silver without softening it, rejects the harmonising proposal that the two writers priced different things, and concludes this is probably the later form of the tradition; Delitzsch refers the question of the price to his note on the older account and explains the answer by fire as the visible assurance that the prayer was heard.

Wesley harmonises the two prices by reading Samuel’s fifty shekels of gold as gold to the value of six hundred shekels of silver, and presses the fire as the figure of substitution, fastening on the sacrifice rather than the sinner; Clarke takes it as proof that God was now pacified towards the king and the people.

debates.question: What did David pay for the threshingfloor?

sides.position: the two figures are obviously discordant, and both look wrong beside the price paid for Machpelah, so perhaps gold should be read as silver; since gold money is not otherwise attested among the Hebrews, this is probably the later form of the story
the accounts can be harmonised: the fifty shekels of gold in Samuel were gold to the value of six hundred shekels of silver
the two writers were pricing different things, Samuel the floor and the oxen, the chronicler the whole temple mount
holders: reported and rejected by Charles Ellicott

sides.position: the question is referred to the note on the parallel account rather than settled here

debates.question: What did the fire from heaven signify?

sides.position: the visible assurance that the prayer was heard and the offering graciously accepted, the sheathed sword being a figure for the stopping of the pestilence
the divine inauguration of a new altar and place of sacrifice, as well as a sign the prayer was heard
proof that God had accepted the man and was now pacified towards him and the people
substitution: the fire that might justly have fastened on the sinner fastened on the sacrifice, as Christ was made sin and a curse for us

outliers: Ellicott alone brings in a Babylonian contract tablet, where a house and grounds fetched the equivalent of six hundred and ninety shekels of silver in the last king of Babylon’s second year.
Ellicott alone endorses Ewald’s principle that it was of the essence of sacrifice to surrender something valued in order to win from God a greater good.
themes: a gift refused so that it may be bought
two prices that will not agree
gold money otherwise unattested
fire as a receipt

27.pericope_label: He put up his sword again into the sheath thereof: why David sacrificed here and not at Gibeon

schools.summary: Gill puts the accepted prayer and the sheathed sword together as two halves of one answer, derives the owner’s name, on Hillerus’s authority, from a word for the pine tree or the ash, is careful that the tabernacle was made by the command of God and according to his direction, and admits plainly that Gibeon was nonetheless the proper place to seek the Lord in.

Ellicott refuses to read the sheathing as mere imagery, since the angel is a real being in both accounts, notes that the word for sheath occurs nowhere else and that a similar Aramaic form may be the true reading, explains that these closing remarks have no counterpart in Samuel and serve to show how a threshingfloor became a permanent sanctuary, and prefers to say that the apparition simply overawed the king.

Clarke makes the fear practical, whether terror of the destroying angel or dread of the delay the journey would cost, and draws the apologetic conclusion that such interventions maintain in the people a full persuasion of their religion; Wesley has the king keeping watch over the city he dared not leave, and reading his accepted sacrifice as warrant for offering more in that place.

debates.question: Is the destroying angel a real being or a figure for the plague?

sides.position: a real concrete being in this account and in the older one alike, so it is hardly fair to call the sheathing a figurative or poetical expression for the cessation of the plague
a personification

debates.question: Why could David not go to Gibeon to enquire of God?

sides.position: because the pestilence was raging at Gibeon
because the vision had struck him with some bodily weakness
because the menacing aspect of the apparition overawed him, leaving an indelible impression of the sanctity of the place where it appeared
because the journey would have delayed the offerings while the people were being exterminated
because he durst not leave Jerusalem while the angel stood over it with drawn sword

outliers: Gill alone presses the owner’s name, the same as the form in Samuel with a small variation of letters, both signifying the ornus, the pine tree or the ash.
Clarke alone draws the apologetic conclusion that such interventions must necessarily maintain in the people a full persuasion of the truth and divine origin of their religion.
themes: a threshingfloor becoming a sanctuary
a tabernacle standing unused at Gibeon
the proper place one cannot reach
a sword put up
